title: What can you say about saw palmetto in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library gives no supported wording for saw palmetto, because no listed source supports one at a dose. Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Improves urine flow in men over 50".

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Improves urine flow in men over 50
wordings_to_avoid.why: FDA's 2000 rule (page 1015) gives this exact phrase as an example of a disease claim.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Treats an enlarged prostate (BPH) or reduces night-time urination
wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a disease and its symptoms.

evidence_gap: Health Canada's monograph lists only condition uses (urinary tract infection symptoms and benign prostatic hyperplasia), which are disease wording in a US review. No other listed source gives a use or dose. The library therefore supports no US wording for saw palmetto.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
